text: IPv4 has about four point three billion possible addresses, nowhere near enough for every phone, laptop, and server on Earth to have its own, let alone every device still being added today. The fix that actually shipped, long before IPv6 saw wide adoption, was NAT — letting an entire private network share just a handful of public IP addresses, often only one.

Here's how it actually works. A router rewrites an internal device's private source address and port to its own public address before sending traffic out, and keeps a NAT table entry for that translation. When the reply comes back, the router looks up the table, rewrites the destination back to the internal device, and delivers it. This port-based variant is called PAT.

A stateless firewall checks every packet in isolation against a fixed rule list, with no memory of what came before — it needs a separate rule for the outbound request and the inbound reply. A stateful firewall tracks active connections instead, and automatically allows the matching reply once it's approved the request, with no second rule needed.

A basic ACL rule evaluates the same handful of fields every time: source, destination, protocol, port, and the action, permit or deny. Rules are read top to bottom, and the first one that matches wins — which is why real rule lists almost always end with an explicit deny-everything-else as the final catch-all.

That closes out Chapter Two, Network Infrastructure and Services — switches, routers, DNS, DHCP, NAT, and basic firewall concepts, the full path a packet takes across a real network and the rules that govern what's allowed through along the way. Chapter Three moves into an entirely different layer: why Linux runs the cloud, starting with the operating system underneath nearly every server you'll ever touch.
